newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI requires central bank assets at market values.
newsitem.headline: EMI requires central bank assets at market values.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute, forerunner of a future European Central Bank, has laid down rules for valuation of assets held by member central banks.
In its 1996 annual report the EMI set out approved accounting principles under which those in the European System of Central Banks are required to value their reserves at market value.
On Friday the EMI declined to comment on the controversy over German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's proposal to revalue the Bundesbank's reserves, including gold and currency.

The move would bring the German central bank's reserve valuation more into line with market levels, as part of efforts to harmonise EU central bank reserve valuations ahead of European economic and monetary union (EMU) scheduled for 1999.
Most other EMU candidates have already adopted a progressive system of revaluing their central bank assets in line with the market and there is no suggestion the German proposals differ.
Details of the EMI requirements as set out in its 1996 annual report, are as follows:

"In 1996, the EMI council approved the accounting principles for the financial reporting of the ESCB. According to these principles the balance sheet will be based on market values, but unrealised gains arising from revaluation will not be recognised as income.

"Unrealised losses will be taken to the profit and loss account if they exceed previous revaluation gains registered in the revaluation account. Such losses may only be reversed on subsequent realisation and not against any future unrealised gains. These principles combine transparency with prudent recognition of income and are appropriate for the nature and conduct of central bank's activities.

"Application of these accounting principles will be mandatory for all items material to the operations of the ESCB, for all items of the ECB's financial statements, and for the calculation of monetary income. Nevertheless, NCB's might continue to draw up and publish their financial statements according to their own accounting rules." -- Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525
